newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Displaced Zaireans cower in fear in Kisangani.
newsitem.headline: Displaced Zaireans cower in fear in Kisangani.

text.p: Zaireans and Rwandan refugees fleeing war in eastern Zaire are cowering in bushes around Kisangani for fear of attack by resentful local people, local aid workers said on Friday.
They also said they were worried by the growing number of Zairean soldiers arriving from the combat zone where the army has lost ground to ethnic Tutsi rebels.

Food is short in Kisangani, a town of 500,000 people in Zaire's remote northeast on the edge of mountains and dense jungle. Fighting has choked supplies and shops have closed after violent protests over government handling of the rebellion.

"What I fear is not what happens if the refugees aren't fed, it's what happens if the army isn't fed," said a local businessman. Army-led looting devastated the capital Kinshasa and other main cities in 1991 and 1993.
Most civilians arriving from the east are Zaireans, stranded in their own country. Some are Hutus from Rwanda and Burundi who fled violence in their homeland over the past three years.
They arrive on swollen legs after trekking from the war zone around Bukavu 500 km (310 miles) further east.
A group of six Zaireans, obviously exhausted, sat in the shade of a tree on a bank of the Zaire River.
"We paid all our money on the way. We can't pay onyone to hide us," said one.
"Go away, you are drawing attention to us," said another.
Jean-Paul Masimana was lucky. The 20-year-old student was able to find a truck to carry him the last 300 km (nearly 200 miles) to Kisangani.
He arrived from Goma in the night with 60 others in the truck and by morning they had dispersed so that they would not be suspected of being Rwandans.
"About 150 km (90 miles) from Goma people started to die, others were too tired to go any further and we left them by the road," Masimana said.
The Zaireans refused to let Hutus walk with them so authorities would not accuse them of being Rwandans themselves.
"All along the road there are cars that have run out of fuel. There is no food, but there is water in the forest, and thousands of people are walking in this direction," Masimana added.
Apart from a few streets where diamond dealers have their brightly painted shops, Kisangani is an overgrown village with tall grass sprouting by sandy roads.
Nobody knows quite how many refugees or displaced Zaireans have yet arrived and are hidden.
The Roman Catholic relief organisation CARITAS is trying to raise money to buy food locally, but supplies are short.
"We might be able to get enough for a week, depending on how many people arrive," said CARITAS official Claude Olenga.
Reports from Lubutu, 200 km (120 miles) further east at the limit of radio contact, say at least 200 vehicles and several thousand people are stranded.
Andrew Hunt of Christian Aid told Reuters in Nairobi that he flew over much of eastern Zaire this week and saw semi-deserted villages and normally busy roads now empty.
He visited Lubutu and met a student, one of about 50 fugitives there from the fighting.

The student, who hitched a ride to Lubutu on a stolen aid vehicle, said several thousand people with ankles swollen from walking and empty stomachs were concentrated in the town of Hombo 90 km (55 miles) west of Bukavu.

Western nations with the means have so far reacted coolly to a French and Spanish proposal for an international force to secure corridors for food aid and passage for the homeless. They include more than a million Hutu refugees dispersed from camps and hundreds of thousands of Zairean villagers.
